To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the accumulation of litter in pure spruce stands compared to pure beech stands is not a direct consequence of the inherent litter recalcitrance, but is a consequence of the adverse environmental conditions in pure spruce compared to pure beeh stands.
the recalcitrant nature of spruce needles is not the main cause for the slow decomposition of spruces in pure spruce stands.

(i) spruce needles decompose at the same rate as beech leaves, (ii) the accumulation of litter in pure spruce stands is caused by adverse environmental conditions, and (iii) mixed beech-spring stands are as effective as pure stands of beech in counteracting adverse environmental conditions.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of how much beech admixture to spruce stands would be necessary to accelerate litter decay and associated nutrient cycling.
the effects of forest tree species mixture within a stand and within a litterbag on litter decomposition.
the impact of tree mixtures on decomposition of leaf litter and nutrient release.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the inherent recalcitance of beech leaves is the reason for higher litter mass remaining under beech compared to spruce.
beech is not superior to spruce, rather both species are equally important in forest nutrient cycling.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the recalcitrant nature of spruce litter is not the reason for the accumulation of litter in pure spruce stands, but that it is the consequence of the low nutrient availability in these stands.
beech litter is not more decomposable than spruce litter and that the litter of both species can be decomposed in similar amounts when mixed together.
the recalcitrant litter of beech is not a good substitute for the recalcitrancy of spruce needles.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the addition of only a small fraction of beech to spruce stands can significantly improve nutrient cycling.
admixing beech to spruce stands may be an effective tool to counteract adverse conditions in pure spruce stands.
the admixture of beech in spruce-dominated stands can increase litter decomposition and the associated nutrient cycling.
